newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - Ancient clan keeps Sri Lanka drum beats alive.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ancient clan keeps Sri Lanka drum beats alive.

text.p: Long before the morning sun clears the distant hills, drum beats that sound like a cannonade break the silence of this sleepy Sri Lankan village.
The drum beats emanate from 70-year-old Kuragala Pinsara's workshop in Weligalle village in the central hill district of Kandy.

Every morning, Pinsara stretches cowhide over hollowed coconut bark, tightens it with a strip of goatskin and slaps the skin with both hands, creating a thunderous rhythm that reverberates down the hillside.
"Aha, now that is the rhythm I was searching for," he beams. "Besides, it will wake up the others."
Pinsara is correct. For soon most of the 300 inhabitants of the village are up too, beating drums that they make to keep alive an ancient tradition on this Indian Ocean island.
Drums have long played an important role in the life of the people of Sri Lanka, their hypnotic rhythms resonating at weddings, funerals and other ceremonial events.
Pinsara, affectionately referred to as "gurunnanse", or guru, is the patriarch of a clan of drum-makers living in Weligalle, about 130 km (80 miles) east of the capital Colombo.
THE DYING ART
Today, the clan is reduced to about 70 families, but its members are among the few remaining traditional craftsmen of Sri Lanka who strive to make a living by practising the craft of their ancestors.
"They are not in it for the money," Pinsara said at his home-cum-workshop.
"You can't make much of a living these days by making and selling traditional drums. It is a desire to keep the traditions alive that keeps us in the business," he said.

These days the ancient craft of drumming is a dying art as the cassette player replaces traditional rhythms at important events and as the younger generation migrates to cities in search of white-collar jobs.
"It is one of those tools of life that a majority of people have absolutely no need for. So our fight is uphill, to keep the art alive and the tradition from dying."
How do they do it?
DRUMS ARE OF ALL KINDS

Pinsara and his clan manufacture traditional drums to order, producing a range of about seven drums that are still in demand. Among them are the "yak bera", or the devil drum, which is used for exorcisms.
The oldest type of drum used in Sri Lanka is the "daula", which is beaten only with specially crafted sticks. Traditionally, the daula was used to announce the time.
Like many old drum-makers, Pinsara supports the idea that nature mysteriously gives drums their distinctive sound.

"In those days, trees found near gushing rivers and waterfalls were preferred for drum-making," he said. "Such trees hear water flowing and absorb those natural sounds. When a tree is struck by lightning, the thunder enters the tree and improves the sound."
THE BEST DRUMS ARE MADE OF MONKEY SKIN

But today, such considerations are a luxury and the drum maker has to make do with any trees that are available. These days, most Sri Lankan drums are made of jak, a yellowish hardwood in plentiful supply, and the bark of coconut, naturally rounded to resemble a drum.
Cowhide or goatskin is used for the drum surfaces. Monkey skin makes the best sound, but it is now prohibited to kill monkeys, Pinsara said.
The guru's 38-year-old son, Kuragala Piyaratne, plans to follow in his father's footsteps and eventually lead the clan of drum-makers.
"People of my age don't do this for a living. but I have been around drums all my life and it will be good if I can spend the rest of my life around them too," he said.
